segments.t: korTTY manages SSH, Mosh and KTPH000local-shellKTPH001 connections through three entry points: KTPH002Quick ConnectKTPH003, the KTPH004Connection ManagerKTPH005, and saved KTPH006ProjectsKTPH007.

Open with KTPH003KTPH001KTPH004+KTPH005KTPH002KTPH006 (or KTPH007Connections → Quick Connect…KTPH008). Enter host, port, username and authentication, and connect without saving. Frequently used connections appear as quick buttons; a live search filters them. Saved connections can be picked from a dropdown with its own search field that matches name, host or KTPH009tagKTPH010 (KTPH000 works as a wildcard); a saved connection's tag is shown next to its name (🏷) in the dropdown and in the quick buttons' tooltips.

KTPH001Connections → Manage Connections…KTPH002 opens a searchable tree of saved connections (optionally grouped); the search field matches name, host, IP address or KTPH003tagKTPH004, with KTPH000 as a wildcard. From here you create, edit, duplicate, delete, tag, import and export connections.
KTPH000ConnectKTPH001 in the Connection Manager signs in to the selected connection in this order:
korTTY checks your organization's KTPH000server access policyKTPH001 first. A blocked server or jump server shows the policy message before korTTY asks you for anything.
A shared KTPH000teamworkKTPH001 connection that names neither a credential nor an SSH key uses the team's default authentication.
A connection with a temporary SSH key reuses that key while it is still valid and asks for a new one once it has expired.
A local shell and SSH key authentication connect without a password.

Otherwise korTTY uses the saved password, from the connection's stored credential first and then from the connection itself, and asks for the password when none is saved; KTPH000OKKTPH001 stays greyed out until you type one. When the saved password is in the locked vault, korTTY first offers KTPH002Unlock Vault…KTPH003 (see KTPH004Unlocking the vault laterKTPH005); if you do not unlock it, korTTY asks you to type the password instead.

Cancelling any of these questions opens no tab. KTPH007DuplicateKTPH008 in a terminal tab's context menu signs in the same way, so it also asks for a new temporary SSH key when the tab's key has expired. A saved or teamwork connection chosen in the KTPH009command paletteKTPH010 (KTPH011KTPH001KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014+KTPH015KTPH003KTPH016, KTPH017KTPH004KTPH018+KTPH019KTPH005KTPH020+KTPH021KTPH006KTPH022 on macOS, then KTPH000 and part of its name) signs in the same way. KTPH023Reopen Closed TabKTPH024 and KTPH025File → Recently ClosedKTPH026 sign in the same way too, with the saved connection as it is now (see KTPH027Working with tabsKTPH028).
The connection editor has these tabs:

Host, port, username, protocol (SSH / Mosh / Local Shell), terminal emulation, KTPH000Character encodingKTPH001 (use default / UTF-8 / ISO-8859-1 / ISO-8859-15 / Windows-1252), authentication (password / key / keyboard-interactive), KTPH002Host key verificationKTPH003 (use default / verify / don't verify), group/folder assignment and an optional free-text KTPH004tagKTPH005. For KTPH006Local ShellKTPH007 connections host, port, username and authentication are not required and are disabled. See KTPH008Character encodingKTPH009.
Per-connection colors, font, ANSI/TrueColor handling, the KTPH000Terminal behaviorKTPH001 section with the KTPH002tab colorKTPH003 and the KTPH004keyword highlightingKTPH005 rule set, terminal effect
Writes this connection's terminal output to a file — folder, format, daily rotation, compression and retention. See KTPH000Terminal loggingKTPH001.
Per-connection KTPH000session journalKTPH001: enable journaling for this connection and configure its capture log and AI summarization
Per-connection AI defaults: the KTPH000AI profileKTPH001 and AI Skills used by terminal AI features on this connection

KTPH000Character encodingKTPH001 sets how korTTY decodes what this connection's session prints and encodes what you type and paste, for servers whose programs still write ISO-8859-1, ISO-8859-15 or Windows-1252 instead of UTF-8. KTPH002Use defaultKTPH003 follows KTPH004Settings → Terminal → EncodingKTPH005 for SSH connections and means UTF-8 for local shells. Mosh only works with UTF-8, so the dropdown is locked for Mosh connections and a note beside it says so. The choice is stored with the connection, survives duplicating, exporting and importing, and applies the next time the tab connects or reconnects.

The KTPH006Terminal behaviorKTPH007 section of the KTPH008Terminal SettingsKTPH009 tab picks the KTPH010keyword highlightingKTPH011 rule set this connection's terminals show: KTPH012Use the defaultKTPH013 follows the default rule set of KTPH014Settings → TerminalKTPH015, KTPH016NoneKTPH017 keeps them plain, or pick a built-in set or one of your own, for example KTPH018Network devicesKTPH019 for switches. The section applies whether or not the connection uses its own terminal settings, and also while terminal effects are switched off. The choice is stored with the connection, survives duplicating, exporting and importing, and saving in the Connection Manager applies it to the connection's open terminals at once. A set chosen for a single pane in a menu or with KTPH020KTPH000KTPH021+KTPH022KTPH001KTPH023+KTPH024KTPH002KTPH025 (KTPH026KTPH003KTPH027+KTPH028KTPH004KTPH029+KTPH030KTPH005KTPH031 on macOS) still wins for that pane.

Every saved connection can carry one optional free-text KTPH003tagKTPH004 — a label such as KTPH000, KTPH001 or a customer name — independent of the group/folder hierarchy. Set it on the connection editor's KTPH005ConnectionKTPH006 tab (next to the group), or in bulk in the Connection Manager. Tags are stored with the connection in KTPH002 and survive duplicating, exporting and importing.

KTPH000VisibleKTPH001 — tagged connections show a 🏷 badge after their name in the Connection Manager tree and in Quick Connect's saved-connections dropdown; the tag also appears in the tooltip of the frequently-used quick buttons.
KTPH000SearchableKTPH001 — the Connection Manager search (local and Teamwork tabs) and Quick Connect's saved-connections search match tags as well as names and hosts.

KTPH000Bulk assign / removeKTPH001 — select one or more servers and choose KTPH002Assign TagKTPH003 from the context menu to tag them in one step. The prompt is pre-filled when all selected connections already share the same tag, and clearing that pre-filled value removes the tag. KTPH004Remove TagKTPH005 clears the tag and is enabled only while the selection contains at least one tagged connection. The same two entries on a folder's context menu apply to every connection in that folder, subfolders included.

KTPH000Export by tagKTPH001 — once at least one tag exists, the Connection Manager's export dialog offers a KTPH002Connections to exportKTPH003 choice: keep the pre-selected connections, or export KTPH004all connections with these tagsKTPH005 — pick one or more tags from the list, the header's connection count follows the selection live, and the export button stays disabled while nothing matches.

A KTPH000tab colorKTPH001 marks every terminal tab of a connection with a small colored dot in front of its title and a 3-pixel frame of the same color around its terminal, so a production server stands out from test machines at a glance. Set it on the connection editor's KTPH002Terminal SettingsKTPH003 tab, in the KTPH004Terminal behaviorKTPH005 section: tick KTPH006Mark this connection's tabs with a colorKTPH007 and pick the color. The picker offers red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple and gray as custom colors, and any other color works too. The section applies whether or not the connection uses its own terminal settings, and it stays when terminal effects are switched off. Untick the box to remove the color.

KTPH001Not by color aloneKTPH002 — pointing at a colored tab shows a tooltip with the connection (KTPH000, or the connection's name for a local shell) and the color by name and code, for example KTPH003Tab color: red (#D32F2F), set on this connectionKTPH004. Screen readers read the same text for the dot.

KTPH000Frame around the terminalKTPH001 — the frame surrounds the whole tab content, all split panes and the status bars included. It takes 3 pixels on each side, so setting or removing a color resizes the connection's open terminals and full-screen programs redraw. To keep only the dot, switch off KTPH002Frame the terminal in its connection's tab colorKTPH003 in the KTPH004Window settingsKTPH005.

KTPH000Applies at onceKTPH001 — saving in the Connection Manager recolors the open tabs of that connection in every window, and removing the color removes the dot and the frame. Tabs opened from a saved connection through Quick Connect, KTPH002DuplicateKTPH003, KTPH004Reopen Closed TabKTPH005 or a KTPH006projectKTPH007 show its color too.

KTPH000Status colors stayKTPH001 — the yellow tab while a connection is being made and the dark red tab of a failed or lost connection work as before; the dot and the frame are shown in addition and never replace them. A pane that KTPH002Split Right (new connection)KTPH003 or KTPH004Split Down (new connection)KTPH005 opened to another server is part of the same tab and sits inside the tab's frame, so it shows the tab's color, not its own.
KTPH002Stored with the connectionKTPH003 — the color is saved in KTPH000 as KTPH001 and survives duplicating, exporting and importing. A value that is not a hex color is ignored.

KTPH000Color from the credential's environmentKTPH001 — a connection without a tab color of its own can take the color of its stored credential's environment, for example red for every connection that signs in with a production credential. Give the environment a color in the Credentials manager under KTPH002Environments...KTPH003, see KTPH004Environments and tab colorsKTPH005. The tooltip then names the environment instead of saying the color is set on the connection, and a color set on the connection always comes first.
Shared connections bring their own color

A KTPH000teamworkKTPH001 connection shows the color written in the shared file, so whoever maintains that file decides how its tabs are marked. That color also comes before the color of your own credential environment. Treat the color as a hint, not as proof of which server you are on: the tooltip still names the connection, and so does the tab title unless you renamed the tab or its KTPH002shell set a titleKTPH003.

Standard SSH via Apache MINA SSHD. Supports password, public-key and keyboard-interactive authentication, keep-alive, and OSC 8 hyperlinks for web and mail addresses that open with KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003 / KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 + click (see KTPH006Links in terminal outputKTPH007).
Roaming, latency-friendly Mosh transport (mosh4j). The Mosh backend is bundled in native builds; existing connections need no migration.

Opens the KTPH000local machine'sKTPH001 shell in a terminal tab (no network) via a pty4j-backed pseudo-terminal. Host, port, username and authentication are not required. See KTPH002Local ShellKTPH003 below.

Interactive Terminal and SFTP connections use the same trust-on-first-use (TOFU) host-key store. Mosh uses it for the SSH bootstrap as well. Trust is keyed by the normalized host name and port, so different saved connections to the same endpoint share one decision.

On the first connection, korTTY shows the key algorithm and OpenSSH SHA-256 fingerprint. Verify that fingerprint with the server administrator before selecting KTPH000YesKTPH001; KTPH002NoKTPH003 is the safe default. A matching key is accepted silently on later connections. If the server presents a different key, korTTY hard-blocks the connection, shows the expected and offered fingerprints, and does not retry because repeating the attempt cannot resolve a possible man-in-the-middle attack. A changed key is never replaced automatically.

When a server was legitimately rebuilt, the changed-key alert of a terminal tab or the SFTP manager offers KTPH001Review and Replace…KTPH002 next to KTPH003CloseKTPH004, which stays the default. The review shows the currently trusted key and the new key, each with its algorithm and SHA-256 fingerprint. KTPH005Replace Key and ConnectKTPH006 stays disabled until you tick KTPH007I have verified the new fingerprint with the server administratorKTPH008, and KTPH009CancelKTPH010 is the default button, so KTPH011KTPH000KTPH012 never confirms. After you confirm, korTTY replaces the trusted key and the same connection continues. The replacement only succeeds while the trusted key is still the one you reviewed: if another window changed or removed it in the meantime, the connection stays blocked and you reconnect to review the current key. A jump server's changed key gets the same review when the connection was opened from a terminal tab or the SFTP manager.

Other connections never offer the replacement, so nothing that runs without your attention waits on a review dialog: the SSH bootstrap of Mosh sessions, remote editors and image viewers restored with a project, and other background transfers. Their alert points to KTPH001Configuration → Security → Known Hosts…KTPH002 instead. While an enterprise policy sets KTPH000, korTTY can neither replace nor remove a trusted key; the alert says so, and your administrator has to update the key.

KTPH000Configuration → Security → Known Hosts…KTPH001 lists every trusted key with host, port, algorithm, SHA-256 fingerprint and the time it was trusted. The search field filters by host, port, algorithm or fingerprint, ignoring case. KTPH002Remove…KTPH003 asks for confirmation, with KTPH004NoKTPH005 as the default, and deletes the key only if it still has the fingerprint shown; the next connection to that server shows the first-use prompt again. If the store cannot be read, the dialog shows the error and offers no actions.

The first-use prompt can be turned off for hosts where it is not wanted — set KTPH000Host key verificationKTPH001 on the connection editor's KTPH002ConnectionKTPH003 tab or in Quick Connect (KTPH004Use defaultKTPH005 / KTPH006VerifyKTPH007 / KTPH008Don't verifyKTPH009), per group via the Connection Manager's group context menu, or globally under KTPH010Settings → TerminalKTPH011. The relaxation is accept-new only: an unknown key is pinned without a prompt, but a key that differs from one already pinned for that host is still hard-blocked. See KTPH012Relaxing host-key verificationKTPH013.

The interactive pins are stored atomically in KTPH000, with cross-process locking so two korTTY windows cannot overwrite each other's decisions. Removing the last trusted key deletes the file, which korTTY treats as an empty store. These endpoint-based pins are separate from the connection-ID-based pins used by unattended JobScheduler SSH, SFTP, and Rsync jobs.

When a new split connection is opened, the SSH handshake runs on a worker while a progress dialog keeps the JavaFX interface responsive. This allows both host-key confirmation and keyboard-interactive authentication to complete without blocking the UI.

A KTPH000Local ShellKTPH001 connection spawns a local pseudo-terminal (PTY) on your own machine instead of connecting to a remote host. It is selectable in both KTPH002Quick ConnectKTPH003 and the KTPH004Connection ManagerKTPH005; for these connections host, port, username and authentication are not required (and are disabled in the dialogs), and no password prompt is shown.

KTPH002PowerShellKTPH003 (default) or KTPH004cmd.exeKTPH005. KTPH006Git BashKTPH007, KTPH008CygwinKTPH009 and KTPH010WSLKTPH011 are also offered as presets — but only when actually installed (Git Bash/Cygwin are detected via their usual install locations / KTPH000; WSL appears only when KTPH001 is present and at least one distribution is installed).
Defaults to your KTPH000 (falling back to KTPH001 or KTPH002).

A free-form KTPH003Custom commandKTPH004 field accepts any executable with arguments (e.g. KTPH000, KTPH001, a Git Bash path), and an optional KTPH005start directoryKTPH006 can be set. The command parser is quote-aware, so shell paths containing spaces — like KTPH002 — launch correctly.

When korTTY runs from its Flatpak package, the local shell is started on the host through KTPH000, including the selected start directory and terminal locale. The package has host-filesystem access so terminal file actions can use host paths. Because the sandbox-side process ID belongs to KTPH001 rather than the host shell, current-directory tracking uses trusted absolute prompt paths instead of reading KTPH002; if no safe host path can be established, path-dependent actions stop with an explicit error.

Terminal logging and recording, plus the AI input/data hooks, work for local shells via a shared KTPH000 interface. Typed and pasted agent requests use the same byte-level input path, and terminal file actions plus local agent runs follow the interactive shell's current directory. macOS/Linux use the local process directory; native PowerShell and cmd use absolute prompt paths. WSL, Git Bash, Cygwin, and custom commands are best-effort when their shell path namespace differs from the host filesystem, and an unmappable directory produces an explicit error instead of a wrong-file fallback. Features that depend on an SSH channel stay SSH-only.
The KTPH000AI AgentKTPH001 and KTPH002AI PlanningKTPH003 also run in local shells on Windows, macOS and Linux — see KTPH004AI assistantKTPH005.
